research_question: What are the evidence-based principles for low-friction, high-trust web/app forms — minimal & forgiving fields, visible persistent labels, marking required vs optional, inline validation that states the requirement, trust signals, field reduction, and respecting the ad->lander->offer journey — and which can be expressed as mechanically-checkable rules for an AI designer building Next.js + Tailwind + Radix/shadcn forms?

phases.name: Landscape
phases.objective: Survey form-usability research: the cost of each field, single-column layout, visible labels over placeholders, top-aligned vs inline labels, required/optional marking, and the psychology of friction vs trust in the conversion funnel.
sub_questions: What does Baymard/NN/g/CXL research say about field count, label placement, and form layout for completion rate?
What is the documented harm of placeholder-as-label and floating-label patterns?
phases.evidence_priorities: Baymard form/checkout research, NN/g form-design articles, CXL form best practices, label-placement eye-tracking.
phases.stop_condition: Complete when the core form-structure rules (single column, visible labels, field minimization, required/optional marking) are enumerated with evidence.

phases.name: Mechanics
phases.objective: How forgiving validation and trust are built: inline validation timing (on-blur not on-keystroke for errors; positive confirmation), error messages that state the requirement and the fix, accessible error association (aria-describedby, aria-invalid, role=alert), autocomplete/inputmode/type for mobile, input formatting tolerance (spaces in card/phone), trust signals near the submit and near sensitive fields, and the ad->lander->offer message-match / no cold-to-offer jump.
sub_questions: What is the optimal inline-validation timing and error-message content per research?
Which HTML/ARIA attributes make a form low-friction AND accessible, and how do mobile keyboards (inputmode, autocomplete) reduce friction?
phases.evidence_priorities: Baymard inline-validation + checkout, MDN autocomplete/inputmode, WAI form tutorial, CXL trust-signal research, Smashing mobile form design.
phases.stop_condition: Complete when validation, error-association, mobile-input, and trust-signal patterns are expressed as checkable rules.

phases.name: Failure Modes
phases.objective: Friction- and trust-killing form defects: placeholder-only labels (vanish on input), unmarked required/optional, validate-on-every-keystroke, vague errors ('invalid input'), errors not tied to the field, too many fields / asking for data not yet needed, no autocomplete/wrong keyboard on mobile, reset-on-error, no submit feedback / double-submit, asking for sensitive data with no trust context, cold ad->offer jump with no message match.
sub_questions: Which form defects most increase abandonment per documented research?
How does each defect manifest on mobile and to assistive-tech users?
phases.evidence_priorities: Baymard abandonment data, NN/g error-message guidance, mobile-form research, checkout-usability findings.
phases.stop_condition: Complete when 10+ distinct friction/trust defects are documented with abandonment mechanism and detection signal.

phases.name: Contrarian
phases.objective: Where form orthodoxy is contested: floating labels vs top-aligned (when acceptable), inline vs after-submit validation edge cases, multi-step vs single-page (does chunking actually help or hide length?), social-proof/trust-badge effectiveness debate, and friction that is GOOD (intentional confirmation for destructive/irreversible actions).
sub_questions: What is the strongest evidence against the 'fewer fields always wins' and 'inline validation always wins' rules?
When is added form friction correct (security, irreversible actions)?
phases.evidence_priorities: Baymard nuance articles, multi-step-form studies, trust-badge A/B debate, intentional-friction literature.
phases.stop_condition: Complete when 2+ substantive counter-arguments are documented with evidence.

openai_instructions: Deduce the minimal-friction form invariants from first principles + research: for any data-collection form, what makes completion most likely while staying accessible and trustworthy. Enumerate checkable assertions (visible persistent label per field, required/optional marked, inline validation that states the requirement, error tied to field via aria, correct input type/inputmode/autocomplete, field-count justification, trust signal near sensitive submit) and the conditions under which each fails.
